name: Motobu · un radar antiaéreo capta algo quieto que luego se aleja
name_en: Motobu · an army radar sees something hang still, then speed off

location.place: Sobre la península de Motobu, norte de Okinawa (hoy Japón)
location.place_en: Over the Motobu Peninsula, northern Okinawa (today Japan)

summary: Hacia las 10:30 del 27 de marzo de 1950, un cabo del 65.º Batallón de Artillería Antiaérea captó con un radar SCR-584, de los que apuntaban los cañones antiaéreos, un único objeto a 13.500 pies sobre la península de Motobu, en Okinawa. Según el informe de inteligencia de la 20.ª Fuerza Aérea, al captarlo estaba inmóvil; luego recorrió 16,9 millas hacia el suroeste en dos minutos, unas 507 millas por hora, hasta que el radar no pudo seguirlo. El radar de Motobu no lo detectó, el del monte Yontan estaba inoperativo y el propio informe anota que cinco F-80 estaban en vuelo. Blue Book lo dejó como no identificado sin pasarlo a sus analistas de radar.
summary_en: At about 10:30 a.m. on March 27, 1950, a corporal of the 65th Anti-Aircraft Artillery Gun Battalion picked up a single object at 13,500 feet over the Motobu Peninsula, Okinawa, on an SCR-584, a radar used to aim anti-aircraft guns. According to the Twentieth Air Force intelligence report, it was stationary when first picked up and then covered 16.9 miles to the south-west in two minutes, about 507 miles per hour, until the radar could no longer track it. The Motobu radar did not detect it, the one on Yontan Mountain was inoperative, and the report itself notes that five F-80s were flying. Blue Book kept it as unidentified without sending it to its radar analysts.

documents.title: Expediente de Blue Book de la península de Motobu, Okinawa (marzo de 1950): tarjeta e informe IR-1-50 de la 20.ª Fuerza Aérea, 3 págs.
documents.title_en: Blue Book file on the Motobu Peninsula, Okinawa (March 1950): record card and Twentieth Air Force report IR-1-50, 3 pp.
documents.description: Las tres hojas del expediente 1950-03-9614443 del Proyecto Blue Book. La primera es la tarjeta (formulario 329, edición de septiembre de 1963): 27 de marzo de 1950, 01:30 Z, fuente militar, un objeto, conclusión «UNIDENTIFIED» con el comentario de que el caso no pasó por los analistas de radar y no consta como propagación anómala ni avería, y el resumen de que el radar no pudo seguir el objeto por su velocidad y de que otro radar de la zona no lo captó. La segunda es la primera parte del formulario AF 112 IR-1-50 de la jefatura adjunta de inteligencia de la 20.ª Fuerza Aérea, muy desvaída: resume el suceso en cuatro apartados legibles a medias y deja leer el asunto («Report of Unidentified Object»), la fecha de la información (27 de marzo de 1950), una fecha de redacción de comienzos de abril, la firma de un coronel, jefe adjunto de inteligencia, el destinatario, el comandante general de las Fuerzas Aéreas del Lejano Oriente, y la lista de los tres anexos (declaración jurada del operador, cuyo apellido se lee a medias, y declaraciones de un oficial de operaciones y de un oficial meteorológico), que no se conservan. La tercera es la segunda parte, legible: posición, tiempo, estación, rumbo, velocidad y altitud del objeto, el radar SCR-584 n.º 754, el aval del comandante del operador, los F-80 en vuelo y los otros dos radares de la isla.
documents.description_en: The three sheets of Project Blue Book file 1950-03-9614443. The first is the record card (Form 329, September 1963 edition): March 27, 1950, 0130Z, military source, one object, conclusion "UNIDENTIFIED" with the comment that the case was not sent to radar analysts and is not recorded as anomalous propagation or malfunction, and the summary that the radar could not track the object because of its speed and that another radar in the area did not pick it up. The second is Part I of AF Form 112 IR-1-50 from the Twentieth Air Force Deputy for Intelligence, badly faded: it summarizes the event in four half-legible paragraphs and shows the subject ("Report of Unidentified Object"), the date of the information (March 27, 1950), a date of preparation in early April, the signature of a colonel, Deputy for Intelligence, the addressee, the Commanding General of the Far East Air Forces, and the list of three enclosures (the affidavit of the operator, whose surname can only be partly read, and statements by an operations officer and a weather officer), which do not survive. The third is Part II, legible: the object's position, weather, station, heading, speed and altitude, SCR-584 radar no. 754, the operator's commanding officer's endorsement, the F-80s in the air and the island's other two radars.

whatHappened:
En marzo de 1950, Okinawa, en las islas Ryukyu, seguía bajo administración militar de Estados Unidos, con bases de la 20.ª Fuerza Aérea y unidades antiaéreas del Ejército. Hacia las 10:30 del 27 de marzo, un cabo del 65.º Batallón de Artillería Antiaérea de cañones manejaba un radar SCR-584 «B», número de serie 754, que según el informe estaba «in good condition»; la tarjeta de Blue Book lo llama «Gun Radar», un radar para apuntar los cañones antiaéreos. Estaba en el parque de artillería de «Kawasake» (así en el documento), a 26° 21′ N y 127° 50′ E. El radar captó un objeto sobre la península de Motobu, en el norte de la isla, a 26° 37′ N y 127° 57′ E, a 13.500 pies de altura (la tarjeta dice 13.000). El informe da una distancia hasta ese primer punto que se lee mal («1…»), y la tarjeta, 18 millas; con esas coordenadas salen unas 20 millas terrestres hacia el nornordeste (cálculo propio). La tarjeta da la hora como 27/0130Z, que es la misma con Okinawa nueve horas por delante de Greenwich (cálculo propio).

Cuando el radar lo captó, el objeto estaba inmóvil. Después se movió con rumbo 220°, hacia el suroeste, a unas 507 millas por hora, cifra que el informe explica así: 16,9 millas entre el primer y el último punto, recorridas en dos minutos. Era un solo objeto, y la última posición fue a 26° 26′ N y, por lo que se lee, 127° 48′ E, a las 10:40. Según el informe, el objeto se «observó» unos diez minutos y el radar lo siguió unos dos minutos después de que empezara a moverse. La tarjeta dice que estuvo inmóvil diez minutos antes de moverse; con el primer contacto a las 10:30, el último a las 10:40 y dos minutos de movimiento, la fase inmóvil del informe dura como mucho unos ocho minutos (cálculo propio).

La tarjeta cuenta cómo se perdió: el radar lo siguió hacia el suroeste hasta un punto sobre una montaña y no pudo seguirlo más allá («to point over a mountain. Could not track beyond this point»). Añade que otro radar de la zona no lo captó y que iba más deprisa de lo que el operador podía seguir («Additional Radar in area did not pick up object. Speed faster than Operator could track»). Un rumbo de 220° durante 16,9 millas desde el primer punto acaba a 26° 26′ N y 127° 46′ E, cerca de la última posición del informe y a unas 6,6 millas del propio radar. Por eso, al final, la antena tenía que girar unos 1,2° por segundo para no perderlo, unas ocho veces más deprisa que al principio (cálculo propio): un objeto rápido que pasa cerca se sigue peor.

El nombre del operador está tachado en el informe. Tenía 36 años, unos quince de servicio militar y llevaba unos veinti… meses como técnico de radar (la segunda cifra no se lee). Su comandante lo consideraba «a superior soldier and radar mechanic and found at all times to be outstandingly reliable and trustworthy». No se tomaron fotografías. A continuación viene una frase subrayada y marcada con una flecha en el margen: cinco cazas F-80 estaban en vuelo y el radar pudo captarlos («One F-80C and 4 F-80's were flying and could have been picked up by radar, at time object was detected»). El informe termina diciendo que la estación de radar de la 20.ª Fuerza Aérea en el monte Yontan estaba fuera de servicio a esa hora y que la de la península de Motobu «did not pick up this object». El tiempo en la zona: estratocúmulos que cubrían 8/10 del cielo entre 3.000 y 4.500 pies, 20 millas de visibilidad, sin precipitación y sin nubes a la altura del objeto.

La primera parte del informe, casi ilegible en el escaneo, coincide con la tarjeta en que el radar dejó de seguir el objeto por su velocidad y lo perdió. Enumera también tres anexos: una declaración jurada del cabo, otra del oficial de operaciones de una unidad de cazas interceptores, la «51st FI…», y otra del oficial meteorológico de un destacamento. Ninguno de los tres se conserva. La tarjeta de Blue Book se rellenó años después, en un formulario de septiembre de 1963, y concluye «UNIDENTIFIED» con este comentario: «Not submitted to Radar Analists at time of receipt in 1950. Track not consistent with A/C. Weather and other causes not apparent. Not recorded as A.P. or malfunction and Operator is considered reliable». Marca como tipo de observación «Ground-Visual» y «Ground-Radar», y como duración «10 Min. (Grnd-Observed)» y «2 Min. (Grnd-Radar)», pero el informe conservado no menciona a nadie que viera el objeto con sus ojos: su apartado h dice «observed» sin distinguir entre la pantalla y la vista.
whatHappened_en:
In March 1950 Okinawa, in the Ryukyu Islands, was still under United States military administration, with Twentieth Air Force bases and Army anti-aircraft units. At about 1030 on March 27, a corporal of the 65th Anti-Aircraft Artillery (AAA) Gun Battalion was operating an SCR-584 "B" radar, serial number 754, which the report says was "in good condition"; the Blue Book record card calls it a "Gun Radar", a radar for aiming anti-aircraft guns. It stood in the gun park at "Kawasake" (so spelled in the document), at 26° 21′ N, 127° 50′ E. The radar picked up an object over the Motobu Peninsula, in the north of the island, at 26° 37′ N, 127° 57′ E, at an altitude of 13,500 feet (the card says 13,000). The report gives a distance to that first point that cannot be read clearly ("1…"), and the card 18 miles; those coordinates give about 20 statute miles to the north-north-east (our own calculation). The card gives the time as 27/0130Z, the same time with Okinawa nine hours ahead of Greenwich (our own calculation).

When the radar picked it up, the object was stationary. Then it moved on a heading of 220°, to the south-west, at about 507 miles per hour, a figure the report explains as follows: 16.9 miles between the first and last points, covered in two minutes. There was only one object, and the last position was at 26° 26′ N and, as far as can be read, 127° 48′ E, at 1040. According to the report, the object was "observed" for about ten minutes and followed by radar for about two minutes after it started to move. The card says it stayed stationary for ten minutes before moving; with first contact at 1030, the last at 1040 and two minutes of movement, the stationary phase in the report lasts at most about eight minutes (our own calculation).

The card tells how it was lost: the radar followed it south-west to a point over a mountain and could go no further ("to point over a mountain. Could not track beyond this point"). It adds that another radar in the area did not pick it up and that it moved faster than the operator could follow ("Additional Radar in area did not pick up object. Speed faster than Operator could track"). A heading of 220° held for 16.9 miles from the first point ends at 26° 26′ N, 127° 46′ E, close to the report's last position and about 6.6 miles from the radar itself. So by the end the antenna had to turn at about 1.2° per second to keep hold of it, some eight times faster than at the start (our own calculation): a fast object passing close is harder to follow.

The operator's name is blacked out in the report. He was 36 years old, had about fifteen years of military service and had been a radar technician for some twenty-… months (the second digit cannot be read). His commanding officer considered him "a superior soldier and radar mechanic and found at all times to be outstandingly reliable and trustworthy". No photographs were taken. Next comes a sentence that is underlined and marked with an arrow in the margin: five F-80 fighters were flying and the radar could have picked them up ("One F-80C and 4 F-80's were flying and could have been picked up by radar, at time object was detected"). The report ends by saying that the Twentieth Air Force radar station on Yontan Mountain was out of service at the time and that the one on the Motobu Peninsula "did not pick up this object". The weather in the area: stratocumulus covering 8/10 of the sky between 3,000 and 4,500 feet, 20 miles visibility, no precipitation and no clouds at the object's height.

Part I of the report, nearly illegible in the scan, agrees with the card that the radar stopped following the object because of its speed and lost it. It also lists three enclosures: an affidavit from the corporal, a statement by the operations officer of a fighter-interceptor unit, the "51st FI…", and another by the weather officer of a detachment. None of the three survives. The Blue Book record card was filled in years later, on a September 1963 form, and concludes "UNIDENTIFIED" with this comment: "Not submitted to Radar Analists at time of receipt in 1950. Track not consistent with A/C. Weather and other causes not apparent. Not recorded as A.P. or malfunction and Operator is considered reliable". It ticks "Ground-Visual" and "Ground-Radar" as the type of observation and gives "10 Min. (Grnd-Observed)" and "2 Min. (Grnd-Radar)" as its length, but the surviving report mentions no one who saw the object with their own eyes: its paragraph h says "observed" without distinguishing between the screen and the eye.
whyMatters:
Los documentos son pocos, pero sus cifras cuadran entre sí: 16,9 millas en dos minutos son 507 millas por hora, y el rumbo y la distancia llevan del primer punto a la latitud que el informe da para el último. El operador tenía el respaldo escrito de su comandante, y la tarjeta anota que la traza no es coherente con un avión, que no hay causas meteorológicas aparentes y que no consta como propagación anómala (cuando capas de aire curvan el haz del radar y le hacen captar cosas lejanas o donde no están) ni como avería. Con esas anotaciones, la tarjeta de Blue Book lo dejó como no identificado.

Los mismos papeles traen los datos en contra. Solo un radar vio el objeto. La estación de Motobu, que estaba en la península sobre la que se captó, no lo detectó, y la de Yontan estaba fuera de servicio, de modo que ningún segundo instrumento lo confirma. Había cinco F-80 en el aire, y el propio informe anota que el radar pudo captarlos, una línea que alguien subrayó y marcó con una flecha. El descarte de Blue Book no salió de un análisis: la misma tarjeta dice que el caso no pasó por sus analistas de radar, y está escrita en un formulario de 1963, más de trece años después. Y el seguimiento se perdió cuando el objeto pasaba cerca del radar, donde algo rápido es más difícil de seguir.

Contra la idea de un avión queda la fase inmóvil: el informe dice que al captarlo el objeto estaba inmóvil, y la tarjeta de 1963 que lo estuvo diez minutos, algo que un F-80 no hace, y nadie en los documentos explica cómo un avión podría producir esa traza. Pero ningún registro de la época excluye los aviones: la frase de la tarjeta se escribió en 1963 sin análisis, y la declaración del oficial de operaciones sobre los vuelos no se conserva. Que lo que estaba inmóvil y lo que se movió no fueran el mismo objeto es una posibilidad que ninguna fuente plantea. Los tres anexos que faltan (la declaración jurada del cabo, la del oficial de operaciones sobre los vuelos y la del oficial meteorológico) son justo los que podrían resolverlo.
whyMatters_en:
The documents are few, but their figures agree with each other: 16.9 miles in two minutes is 507 miles per hour, and the heading and distance lead from the first point to the latitude the report gives for the last. The operator had his commanding officer's written backing, and the card notes that the track is not consistent with an aircraft, that no weather causes are apparent and that it is not recorded as anomalous propagation (when layers of air bend the radar beam and make it pick up distant things or show them where they are not) or as a malfunction. With those notes, the Blue Book card kept it as unidentified.

The same papers hold the data against it. Only one radar saw the object. The Motobu station, located on the peninsula over which it was picked up, did not detect it, and the Yontan station was out of service, so no second instrument confirms it. Five F-80s were in the air, and the report itself notes that the radar could have picked them up, a line someone underlined and marked with an arrow. Blue Book's dismissal did not come from an analysis: the same card says the case was not sent to its radar analysts, and it is written on a 1963 form, more than thirteen years later. And the track was lost as the object passed close to the radar, where anything fast is harder to follow.

Against the idea of an aircraft stands the stationary phase: the report says the object was stationary when first picked up, and the 1963 card that it stayed so for ten minutes, which an F-80 does not do, and no one in the documents explains how an aircraft could produce that track. But no record of the period excludes the aircraft: the card's sentence was written in 1963 without analysis, and the operations officer's statement on the flights does not survive. That the thing that hung still and the thing that moved were not the same object is a possibility that no source raises. The three missing enclosures (the corporal's affidavit, the operations officer's statement on the flights and the weather officer's) are exactly the ones that could settle it.
evidence: Formulario AF 112 IR-1-50, segunda parte (20.ª Fuerza Aérea): objeto captado hacia las 10:30 del 27 de marzo de 1950 a 26° 37′ N, 127° 57′ E, a 13.500 pies; inmóvil al principio, luego rumbo 220° a unas 507 millas por hora (16,9 millas en dos minutos); última posición a las 10:40.
El mismo informe: radar SCR-584 «B», n.º de serie 754, «in good condition», en el parque de artillería de «Kawasake» (26° 21′ N, 127° 50′ E); sin fotografías.

El operador, un cabo del 65.º Batallón de Artillería Antiaérea (APO 331) de 36 años y unos quince de servicio, con su nombre tachado; su comandante lo califica de «outstandingly reliable and trustworthy».
El informe anota, subrayado y con una flecha en el margen: «One F-80C and 4 F-80's were flying and could have been picked up by radar, at time object was detected».
El radar de la 20.ª Fuerza Aérea en el monte Yontan estaba inoperativo y la estación de radar de la península de Motobu «did not pick up this object».

La primera parte del formulario enumera tres anexos que no se conservan: la declaración jurada del cabo y las declaraciones del oficial de operaciones de la «51st FI…» y del oficial meteorológico de un destacamento.

Tarjeta de Blue Book (formulario de septiembre de 1963): «UNIDENTIFIED»; «Not submitted to Radar Analists at time of receipt in 1950. Track not consistent with A/C. Weather and other causes not apparent. Not recorded as A.P. or malfunction and Operator is considered reliable». Sobre la pérdida del objeto: «Could not track beyond this point», «Additional Radar in area did not pick up object. Speed faster than Operator could track».

evidence_en: AF Form 112 IR-1-50, Part II (Twentieth Air Force): object picked up at about 1030 on March 27, 1950 at 26° 37′ N, 127° 57′ E, at 13,500 feet; stationary at first, then heading 220° at about 507 miles per hour (16.9 miles in two minutes); last position at 1040.
Same report: SCR-584 "B" radar, serial no. 754, "in good condition", in the "Kawasake" gun park (26° 21′ N, 127° 50′ E); no photographs.

The operator, a corporal of the 65th AAA Gun Battalion (APO 331), aged 36 with about fifteen years' service, his name blacked out; his commanding officer rates him "outstandingly reliable and trustworthy".
The report notes, underlined and with an arrow in the margin: "One F-80C and 4 F-80's were flying and could have been picked up by radar, at time object was detected".
The Twentieth Air Force radar on Yontan Mountain was inoperative and the radar station on the Motobu Peninsula "did not pick up this object".
Part I of the form lists three enclosures that do not survive: the corporal's affidavit and statements by the operations officer of the "51st FI…" and by the weather officer of a detachment.

Blue Book record card (September 1963 form): "UNIDENTIFIED"; "Not submitted to Radar Analists at time of receipt in 1950. Track not consistent with A/C. Weather and other causes not apparent. Not recorded as A.P. or malfunction and Operator is considered reliable". On the loss of the object: "Could not track beyond this point", "Additional Radar in area did not pick up object. Speed faster than Operator could track".
1950 Blue Book index: no. 678, March 27, "Motubu, Okinawa", "Military RADAR", "UNIDENTIFIED".

classBasis.es: La única causa del expediente está en el informe IR-1-50, subrayada y con una flecha al margen: «One F-80C and 4 F-80's were flying and could have been picked up by radar». El tramo en movimiento, 16,9 millas en dos minutos, es compatible con un avión, y ningún registro de la época lo excluye: se ha perdido la declaración del oficial de operaciones sobre los vuelos, anexa al informe. En contra: el informe dice que el blanco estaba inmóvil al captarlo, y la tarjeta, que lo estuvo diez minutos, algo que un avión no hace; y anota «Track not consistent with A/C», en un formulario de 1963, aunque según ella el caso nunca pasó por los analistas de radar. Propuesta débil y en disputa, no refutada.
classBasis.en: The only cause in the file is in report IR-1-50, underlined and marked with an arrow in the margin: "One F-80C and 4 F-80's were flying and could have been picked up by radar". The moving leg, 16.9 miles in two minutes, is compatible with an aircraft, and no record of the period excludes it: the operations officer's statement on the flights, enclosed with the report, has been lost. Against it: the report says the target was stationary when first picked up, and the card that it stayed so for ten minutes, which an aircraft does not do; and it notes "Track not consistent with A/C", on a 1963 form, although by its own account the case never went to radar analysts. A weak, disputed proposal, not a refuted one.
